subtopic_detail: Impending obstruction with stridor at rest and marked recession
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing an 18 month old boy with 2 days of barking cough now with continuous stridor at rest, marked sternal recession, agitation, and mottled peripheries. Saturations are 91 percent on 4 L Hudson mask. Weight is 12 kg. Temperature is 38.2. He has not received prior steroids. He is drooling minimally with no fever until this morning, and had been fully immunised. No foreign body history reported by parents.

The anaesthetist and ENT team are aware and coming to the department.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 56 with marked recession, SpO2 91% on 4 L Hudson, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius, GCS 14 agitated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back to back and oral ibuprofen and paracetamol for fever without steroid therapy
options.rationale: Salbutamol has no role in croup because obstruction is subglottic oedema, not bronchospasm; steroids are the cornerstone therapy. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: IV cefotaxime 50 mg per kg 8 hourly empirically and lateral neck X-ray urgently to exclude epiglottitis
options.rationale: Barking cough with viral prodrome is classic croup, not epiglottitis; distressing the child for X-ray in impending obstruction can precipitate complete airway loss. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg alone and observe on the ward for 4 hours before reassessment for adrenaline
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest needs nebulised adrenaline immediately for airway oedema; oral prednisolone alone acts too slowly and observation risks obstruction. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 1 in 1000 5 mL, oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg, minimise handling, and prepare for possible intubation
options.rationale: Severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession is treated with nebulised adrenaline for immediate airway oedema relief, corticosteroids (dexamethasone) for sustained benefit, minimal handling to avoid distress, and anaesthetic and ENT standby for intubation if needed. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

options.text: Insert IV line and give bolus IV hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg and 20 mL per kg saline before any nebulised treatment
options.rationale: Distressing the child with IV access in impending obstruction can precipitate airway loss; oral or IM dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline are preferred first steps. (Source: RCH Melbourne Croup Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe croup with stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxia is treated with nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone. Minimise handling to avoid worsening obstruction. Anaesthetic and ENT standby is essential in impending failure. Bronchodilators have no role and epiglottitis is rare in immunised children. IV access in a distressed child should be delayed until the airway is secured or improving.
key_points: Severe croup: nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (max 12 mg) or IM if unable to swallow
Minimise handling, no unnecessary investigations, ENT plus anaesthetics standby
Salbutamol and antibiotics not indicated in typical viral croup
explanation.pearls: RCH Melbourne uses dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg oral (up to 12 mg) as first line; prednisolone 1 mg per kg per day for 3 days is an alternative but with slightly higher relapse rate; observation for at least 3 to 4 hours after adrenaline to detect rebound.

subtopic_detail: 17 year old cannabis user with 3 months of delusions and functional decline
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 17 year old boy referred by his GP with 3 months of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and withdrawal from school. He has been using cannabis 4 times a week since age 15. His mother describes him as flat, suspicious, and staying awake at night. There is no substance intoxication currently and no acute suicidality or violence. He has no medical comorbidity. Physical examination and bloods are normal. He is engaged with his mother and willing to try treatment.

He is being seen in the Early Intervention Service outpatient clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, urine drug screen positive cannabis only, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, prolactin 320 mIU/L (males under 350)
data_table.Imaging: MRI brain unremarkable, ECG QTc 400 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: SSRI sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first line because cannabis-induced anxiety underlies the presentation
options.rationale: SSRIs do not treat psychotic symptoms and may worsen them in cannabis induced psychosis; antipsychotic therapy plus cessation support is standard first line. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Olanzapine 20 mg orally at night at full target dose from day one to control positive symptoms rapidly
options.rationale: Olanzapine at high starting dose has significant metabolic risk (weight, glucose, lipids) in adolescents; start low and titrate slowly, and it is not first choice for FEP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Haloperidol 10 mg orally daily and lithium 800 mg orally at night for mood stabilisation as first therapy
options.rationale: First generation antipsychotics have higher extrapyramidal side effects than second generation, and adding lithium without a clear mood diagnosis is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night and titrate over 2 weeks alongside weekly full blood count monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; it is not first line in FEP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg orally at night with slow titration to 2 to 4 mg daily, plus psychosocial support in EIS
options.rationale: First episode psychosis in adolescents is treated with low dose second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone 1 to 4 mg or aripiprazole 5 to 15 mg) with slow titration to minimise side effects, alongside evidence based psychosocial intervention through EIS. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guideline)

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis in adolescents is treated with a low dose second-generation antipsychotic (typically risperidone or aripiprazole) titrated slowly, alongside psychosocial intervention through the Early Intervention Service. Olanzapine is avoided as first line due to metabolic side effects. Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance. Baseline metabolic parameters and ECG are checked and monitored. Cannabis cessation support is essential.
key_points: First line: low dose second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole)
Start low, titrate slowly, watch metabolic and EPS side effects
Clozapine after 2 adequate antipsychotic trials fail
EIS provides case management, family work, and CBTp
explanation.pearls: RANZCP recommends baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, and ECG before starting antipsychotic; risperidone dose in adolescents starts 0.5 to 1 mg, target 2 to 4 mg, higher doses give more EPS without extra efficacy.

subtopic_detail: CIWA 22 with tremor and tachycardia at day 2
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultation liaison registrar reviewing a 52 year old man 36 hours after admission to a medical ward for pancreatitis. He drinks 200 g alcohol daily. He is tremulous, sweating, agitated, and disoriented to time. Heart rate is 128 and blood pressure 168/98. He has had a single 5 mg IV diazepam so far. CIWA-Ar score is now 22. Blood alcohol is zero. He has no seizure yet. Magnesium is 0.62, potassium 3.4. He is nil by mouth for pancreatitis.

The medical team asks about withdrawal management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees Celsius, weight 82 kg
data_table.Bloods: sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), lipase 780 U/L (10-60), CK 240 U/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV diazepam 10 mg boluses every 15 minutes until CIWA under 10, plus IV thiamine 300 mg daily and magnesium replacement
options.rationale: Severe alcohol withdrawal is treated with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (front loading with IV diazepam boluses), IV high dose thiamine before any glucose, and correction of magnesium and potassium to reduce seizure and DT risk. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg 6 hourly fixed schedule for 5 days and oral thiamine 100 mg once daily
options.rationale: Oral fixed schedule is inappropriate when nil by mouth for pancreatitis, and low oral thiamine dose is insufficient in high risk withdrawal; symptom-triggered IV benzodiazepine and high dose parenteral thiamine are indicated. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg IM to sedate the agitation without further benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the primary agent for alcohol withdrawal management. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV dextrose 50 percent 50 mL bolus first for hypoglycaemia risk then thiamine 100 mg IV over 2 hours after
options.rationale: Giving glucose before thiamine in a chronic alcohol user risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must be given first or concurrently. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV clonidine 150 mcg boluses only to lower blood pressure and pulse, without benzodiazepine or thiamine therapy
options.rationale: Clonidine treats autonomic symptoms but not seizure or delirium risk; it is adjunctive at most, benzodiazepines and thiamine are essential first line. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe alcohol withdrawal is managed with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (front-loaded diazepam boluses to CIWA-Ar under 10), IV thiamine before or with any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and correction of magnesium and potassium. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are not first line. Clonidine treats autonomic symptoms but not seizures or delirium. Anti-emetics may be used adjunctively.
key_points: Benzodiazepines are first line for alcohol withdrawal (diazepam or lorazepam)
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3 to 5 days before any glucose
Correct magnesium and potassium to reduce seizure risk
Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are not first line
explanation.pearls: CIWA-Ar over 15 signals severe withdrawal; diazepam has long active metabolites providing smooth taper, lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment; risk factors for DTs include prior DT or seizure, tachycardia over 120, systolic BP over 160, and high blood alcohol on presentation still drinking.

subtopic_detail: Generalised tonic clonic seizure at day 3 of withdrawal on the ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to a 60 year old man on day 3 of an admission for alcohol withdrawal. He has just had a witnessed 90 second generalised tonic clonic seizure. He is now post-ictal and confused with GCS 12. He was on oral diazepam 10 mg 6 hourly as needed. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, and tachycardic. He has had no vomiting and airway is patent. Point of care glucose is 4.6 and sodium is 132. Magnesium is 0.55. He has no head injury. He is being nursed in a general medical bay.

The consultant is on their way. You must act now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 172/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 12 post-ictal
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.55 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), ethanol 0 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain arranged non-urgently after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg per kg loading dose infused over 30 minutes and continue oral diazepam as previously prescribed
options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for alcohol withdrawal seizures because the mechanism is GABA hypofunction, not neuronal hyperexcitability; benzodiazepine is first line. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV lorazepam 4 mg bolus now with airway support, IV thiamine 300 mg, IV magnesium 10 mmol over 1 hour, transfer to HDU
options.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal seizure is treated with IV benzodiazepine, high dose parenteral thiamine, magnesium and potassium replacement, and escalation of care due to DT risk; lorazepam has active metabolites less affected by hepatic dysfunction. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV levetiracetam 60 mg per kg loading dose alone and no additional benzodiazepine for the withdrawal seizure now
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is used in status epilepticus of other causes; alcohol withdrawal seizure needs benzodiazepine, not levetiracetam as sole therapy. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV thiopental 3 mg per kg for immediate seizure abortion and paralysis with rocuronium for tracheal intubation
options.rationale: Thiopental induction and paralysis is not indicated for a single self-terminated withdrawal seizure with intact airway; benzodiazepine and supportive care are the correct step. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg and lorazepam 1 mg IM to manage agitation, and defer thiamine until confirmed nutritional status
options.rationale: Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold; withholding thiamine risks Wernicke encephalopathy. Prompt IV thiamine is essential in this scenario. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures are treated with IV benzodiazepines (lorazepam or diazepam), high dose parenteral thiamine, and correction of magnesium and potassium. Phenytoin and levetiracetam do not treat the underlying GABA hypofunction and are ineffective. Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are avoided. After a withdrawal seizure the risk of DTs and further seizures rises so escalation to HDU is prudent.
key_points: First line for withdrawal seizure: IV benzodiazepine
IV thiamine 300 mg before or with any glucose
Correct magnesium and potassium promptly
Phenytoin and levetiracetam are not effective for withdrawal seizures
explanation.pearls: Prior withdrawal seizure is the strongest single risk factor for DTs (risk about 3 fold); RACGP suggests loading IV diazepam 20 mg every 20 minutes up to 100 mg or lorazepam 4 mg every 15 minutes titrated to symptoms; consider phenobarbitone for benzodiazepine resistant DTs in ICU.

subtopic_detail: Persistent orofacial dyskinesia after 5 years of antipsychotic therapy
stem:
You are the community psychiatrist reviewing a 58 year old woman with schizophrenia stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 5 years. She has developed persistent tongue protrusion, lip smacking, and choreoathetoid movements of her fingers over the past 6 months. The Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score is 12. She has not had recent dose changes. She is not depressed and functioning well socially. Reducing or switching antipsychotic in the past has caused relapse. She is on no other movement affecting medication.

She finds the movements distressing.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 76 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, calcium and copper normal, HbA1c 41 mmol/mol, prolactin 620 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily and continue current antipsychotic without switching agent
options.rationale: Propranolol treats akathisia, not tardive dyskinesia; it has no established role in TD reduction. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Add oral benztropine 2 mg orally twice daily as anticholinergic therapy for the involuntary movements now
options.rationale: Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia; they are used for acute dystonia or parkinsonism only and are contraindicated in TD. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Add valbenazine 40 mg orally once daily, uptitrate to 80 mg after 1 week if tolerated and monitor for sedation
options.rationale: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are first line evidence based treatment for moderate to severe tardive dyskinesia; they reduce AIMS scores with tolerable side effects. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Increase risperidone dose to 6 mg orally daily to suppress the movements and manage residual psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Increasing the offending agent temporarily masks TD but worsens the underlying process; long term worsening is expected and it is not standard care. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

options.text: Switch to clozapine 12.5 mg orally at night with weekly full blood count first line as best option for TD control
options.rationale: Clozapine may be considered when TD coexists with treatment resistant psychosis, but is not first line for TD when the patient is stable on current antipsychotic; VMAT2 inhibitor is first line. (Source: APA Schizophrenia Guideline 2020)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia after long term antipsychotic use is treated first line with a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) when clinically significant. Anticholinergics worsen TD and propranolol treats akathisia, not TD. Increasing the offending antipsychotic worsens TD long term. Clozapine may help when TD coexists with treatment resistant psychosis. Regular AIMS monitoring guides therapy.
key_points: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are first line for TD
Anticholinergics worsen TD
Increasing the offending antipsychotic worsens TD long term
AIMS monitoring at baseline and 3 to 6 monthly on antipsychotic
explanation.pearls: Valbenazine dose 40 mg starting, uptitrate to 80 mg after 1 week, watch for somnolence, QTc prolongation and parkinsonism; deutetrabenazine 6 mg twice daily starting, target 18 to 24 mg twice daily; monitor AIMS every 3 months on treatment.

subtopic_detail: Severe depression with psychosis and food refusal, prior medication failure
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman admitted involuntarily for severe depression with mood congruent psychotic delusions of decay and 4 weeks of food and fluid refusal. She has lost 12 kg. She has failed adequate trials of sertraline and mirtazapine over 6 months. She is now dehydrated, bradycardic, and mute. Blood tests show mild AKI. She has capacity assessed as impaired for treatment decisions. Her adult daughter is her formally appointed medical treatment decision maker and consents to ECT. There are no contraindications.

An anaesthetist has assessed her and approves ECT under general anaesthetic.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, weight 52 kg (was 64 kg)
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 128 umol/L (45-90), ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 420 ms
data_table.Imaging: CT brain no acute pathology or mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: IV ketamine 0.5 mg per kg over 40 minutes weekly in outpatient clinic as first line therapy after medication failure
options.rationale: Ketamine for depression is second line and not established for severe depression with psychosis; safety in acute inpatient severe illness is limited compared with ECT. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Trial venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily uptitrating over 4 weeks before considering electroconvulsive therapy referral
options.rationale: In severe depression with psychosis, food refusal, and medication failure, further oral antidepressant trial delays life-saving treatment; ECT has response within 2 to 3 weeks and is first line here. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Add lithium 400 mg orally at night augmentation of current SSRI as first step before any ECT is considered
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is one option in TRD, but not appropriate as first step when the patient is deteriorating rapidly with food refusal; ECT is faster acting and indicated. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: Start twice weekly bitemporal ECT with 6 to 12 sessions expected, rehydrate first, prescribe pre-ECT metoclopramide and monitor cognition
options.rationale: Severe depression with psychosis, food refusal, and medication failure is a strong indication for ECT; twice weekly bitemporal or high dose right unilateral is standard; rehydration and pre-ECT preparation reduce anaesthetic risk. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

options.text: IV clomipramine 25 mg daily infusion titrated up over 10 days as intravenous antidepressant instead of ECT
options.rationale: IV clomipramine is not standard in Australia and lacks evidence over oral therapy or ECT; ECT is faster and safer in this clinical picture. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe depression with psychotic features, catatonia, food refusal, or high suicide risk after failed medication trials is a first line indication for ECT, which acts within 2 to 3 weeks. Bitemporal placement gives fastest and most potent effect but with more cognitive side effects; high dose right unilateral is an alternative with less memory impact. Rehydration and pre-ECT assessment reduce anaesthetic risk. Ongoing maintenance may be pharmacological or continuation ECT.
key_points: First line ECT indications: severe depression with psychosis, catatonia, food refusal, high suicide risk
Response usually within 6 to 12 sessions, given twice weekly
Bitemporal fastest response, right unilateral less cognitive impact
Consent required from patient or medical treatment decision maker if impaired
explanation.pearls: RANZCP audit shows response rates 60 to 80 percent in TRD; number needed to treat around 2 for remission in severe psychotic depression; short term memory effects usually resolve in 6 months, long term autobiographical gaps rare with unilateral placement.

subtopic_detail: Chronic post traumatic stress with dissociation after childhood abuse
stem:
You are the psychiatry consultant reviewing a 34 year old woman with 10 years of intrusive memories, dissociative episodes, chronic nightmares, hyperarousal, and unstable relationships since childhood sexual abuse. She has tried sertraline for 6 months at 200 mg with partial response. She is stable psychosocially with supportive partner and no active substance use. She has no current suicidal intent but self-harmed 6 months ago. She wants to reduce dissociation and nightmares. She has read about EMDR and asks whether it might help her.

She is engaged and prefers a structured psychological approach.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, weight 68 kg
data_table.Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT normal, HbA1c 34 mmol/mol, no substance use on urine screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Refer for supportive counselling only and continue current sertraline without additional pharmacological or psychological therapy
options.rationale: Non-trauma focused counselling has weaker evidence than TF-CBT or EMDR in PTSD; the recommended approach is trauma focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Switch sertraline to venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily and add quetiapine 100 mg at night for dissociation control
options.rationale: Second SSRI or SNRI switch is reasonable in nonresponse but should be paired with trauma focused therapy; quetiapine is not first line for dissociation and adds metabolic risk without established PTSD benefit. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Start clonazepam 0.5 mg at night for hyperarousal and defer psychological therapy until symptoms are controlled first
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and impair trauma processing; they are contraindicated as monotherapy in PTSD. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg at night for sleep and continue sertraline without any psychological intervention referral
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy alone leaves PTSD undertreated; trauma focused psychological therapy is the strongest evidence based treatment and should be offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy (either EMDR or trauma focused CBT), and add prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares
options.rationale: Trauma focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT or EMDR) are first line for PTSD in Australian and international guidelines, alongside SSRI; prazosin is second line adjunct for trauma nightmares in adults. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: PTSD treatment in adults is trauma focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR) as first line, with SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) or venlafaxine as pharmacological options. Prazosin is a second line adjunct for trauma related nightmares. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated. Complex PTSD after childhood trauma may need longer and phased therapy. Supportive counselling alone has weaker evidence than trauma focused approaches.
key_points: First line: trauma focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR)
Pharmacological first line: SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine
Prazosin second line adjunct for trauma related nightmares
Avoid benzodiazepines: worsen PTSD outcomes
explanation.pearls: Phoenix Australia recommends 8 to 12 sessions of TF-CBT or EMDR for uncomplicated PTSD, phased approach with stabilisation before trauma processing in complex PTSD; prazosin start 1 mg at night, titrate to 2 to 6 mg for nightmares, watch first-dose hypotension.
